newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks dragged lower by technology shares.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks dragged lower by technology shares.

text.p: Wall Street stocks fell Wednesday as the market took its cue from weakness in high-technology shares.
At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 46.07 points at 6,850.49 after earlier losing more than 50 points.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances by a 2-1 margin on active New York Stock Exchange volume of 311 million shares.
The Nasdaq composite index, which is laced with technology stocks, sank 23.67 points to 1,245.67. The American Stock Exchange index fell 3.40 to 592.05.

Networking stocks drove the sell-off on reports of slowing Internet equipment sales and comments by Barton Biggs, chairman of Morgan Stanley's asset management department, that a bear market has begun for the high technology issues.

"We are getting into a capitulation stage in the techs. They have been correcting for months, we are now at the point when investors have started recognising this and are throwing in the towel," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
Blumberg said the technology shares are overextended and fundamentally expensive.
"There are some great companies that are overpriced and are now getting closer to fair values," he said. "They probably won't become buys until they are below fair value."
The techs, passing through a seasonally weak period to begin with, were hit by Bigg's bearish comments in a Wall Street Journal article.

"In real terms a bear market has begun," Biggs said. "I believe the tech cycle has peaked ... Orders and shipments won't decline. But the rate of growth will slow to 10 percent from 20 or 25 percent."

Cisco Systems Inc., the biggest networking company, topped the Nasdaq most-active list, falling 2-3/8 to 48. Ascend Communications Inc. was down 4-3/4 at 43-3/8. Microsoft Corp. fell four to 95-5/8 and International Business Machines Corp. lost three to 136-3/8.
"The techs were leaders on the upside and this sell-off has demoralised the overall market," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

Analysts said that volatility ahead of Friday's triple-witching expirations and ongoing anxiety ahead of the March 25 meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee contributed to the market's volatility.
